name: Conjugated linoleic acid (CLA)

lead: Conjugated linoleic acids are fatty acids found mainly in meat and dairy from cattle and sheep. Supplements are sold for fat loss and as a bodybuilding aid, aimed at a leaner physique.

Interest began with late-1990s mouse experiments that reported large drops in body fat, linked to the t10,c12 isomer. Human trials have generally shown much smaller effects, and a 2012 meta-analysis found no long-term effect on body composition in overweight or obese people.

paras: It is taken as softgel capsules, usually within a cutting routine of diet and training. Products differ in isomer mix, and results in trials have been small or short-lived.

A 2018 meta-analysis of randomised trials reported that CLA supplementation may raise C-reactive protein and TNF-alpha, markers of inflammation. The US FDA categorised CLA as generally recognised as safe for use in foods in 2008. Long-term effects in humans remain under study.

angle.text: Users take CLA, a fatty acid found in ruminant meat and dairy, to shift fat storage and get leaner. Mouse studies reported large body-fat drops, while human trials measuring body composition report small or short-lived changes.

lead: Conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) refers to a group of positional and geometric isomers of linoleic acid whose double bonds are conjugated. The most abundant forms are cis-9,trans-11 (rumenic acid) and trans-10,cis-12. They occur naturally in the meat and dairy fat of ruminants, produced by rumen microbes. [1][2]

CLA became a weight-management supplement after a 1997 mouse study reported 57 to 60 percent lower body fat in animals fed a CLA-supplemented diet. [3] A later mouse study attributed the body-composition changes to the trans-10,cis-12 isomer. [4]

Human trials have been less dramatic. Wikipedia reports that a 2012 systematic review and meta-analysis found no long-term effect on body composition in overweight or obese people, and that a 2018 meta-analysis found CLA supplementation may increase inflammatory markers. [1]

Cutting stacks; grass-fed beef and butter [13][14]

paras: About 28 isomers are possible in principle. In CLA the two double bonds are separated by a single bond rather than the usual two, and isomers differ in position and cis/trans geometry. [1] Ruminant microbes create CLA and its precursor trans-vaccenic acid, and tissues including the mammary gland can convert vaccenic acid to c9,t11-CLA through the enzyme delta-9 desaturase, as shown in dairy cows. [1][5]

Meat and milk from grass-fed ruminants contain more CLA than those from grain-fed animals. [1] Reviews of milk-fat synthesis describe how some diets alter rumen biohydrogenation and reduce milk fat, with the trans-10,cis-12 isomer implicated. [6]

Wikipedia also lists eggs from CLA-fed hens, some mushrooms, and, in rats, conversion of pomegranate seed punicic acid to rumenic acid as additional sources, and notes that gut bacteria such as Bifidobacterium can make CLA from linoleic acid. [1]

sections.h: Origins and rise as a supplement
paras: Wikipedia dates the start of research on CLA's biological activity to work showing that it inhibited chemically induced cancer in mice, with the page citing a 1987 paper by Ha, Grimm and Pariza for the finding. [1] That anticancer line of research produced a long literature on CLA-enriched foods such as meat, dairy products and eggs, reviewed in cell and animal studies. [7]

The body-composition story begins with a 1997 mouse report in which animals eating a diet with 0.5 percent CLA showed 57 and 60 percent lower body fat and 5 and 14 percent higher lean mass than controls, along with higher carnitine palmitoyltransferase activity. [3] Follow-up work in 1999 attributed the body-composition changes to the trans-10,cis-12 isomer rather than the c9,t11 form that dominates dietary sources. [4] Review articles in the early 2000s described how CLA is metabolised and how the two main isomers differ in biological activity. [8][9]

Those results gave supplement makers a ready-made pitch: a fatty acid from beef and butter that might shift the body toward lean mass. By the mid-2000s CLA appeared in lists of fat-metabolism supplements discussed in sports-nutrition reviews and in bodybuilding forums. [10][11]

CLA is sold as a supplement to people who want to reduce body fat and keep lean mass, marketed for bodybuilding as well as anticancer and cardiovascular purposes; Wikipedia notes that clinical studies have not confirmed a medical use. [1] The appearance chain is leaner midsection and more definition through modest fat loss.

Research on the t10,c12 isomer has examined its effects on body fat. [4] A 2012 meta-analysis of trials in overweight and obese adults, as summarised on Wikipedia, found no long-term body composition effect. [1]

Supplements are typically softgels of CLA mixed isomers, often marketed as fat burners or alongside bodybuilding and cutting stacks, and sometimes combined with caffeine, green tea or carnitine in multi-ingredient products. A 2011 review of fat-burner supplements listed CLA among popular ones and concluded that caffeine and green tea had supporting data while evidence for many others, CLA included, was lacking. [10] Memorial Sloan Kettering's patient page describes marketed claims of weight loss, cholesterol lowering and cancer prevention, and links the t10,c12 isomer mainly with anti-obesity effects and c9,t11 mainly with anticancer effects. [12]

CLA has been discussed on strength-training forums since at least the early 2000s, usually in two forms: as a softgel supplement and as a reason to prefer particular foods. On T Nation, one 2003 thread about butter describes it as a fat source rich in CLA with anticancer properties, and a 2008 thread on grass-fed beef sits within the wider argument that grass-fed animal products contain more of it. [13][14] A 2005 thread quotes a review of CLA isomers and lipolysis, and a 2004 guest-forum thread with nutrition coach John Berardi quotes a 2003 Journal of Lipid Research review of CLA for obesity that notes how widely the supplements are promoted as weight-loss agents. [11][15]

Some posters list CLA capsules as one component of a diet plan alongside fish oil, flax oil and carbohydrate manipulation for cutting, a pattern that treats CLA as one small part of a stack. [16] A 2009 protein-intake thread lists conjugated linoleic acids among nutrients said to provide auxiliary support for performance and muscle growth. [17] More recent threads, such as a 2022 one on animal trans fats and heart health, show the discussion moving to whether ruminant trans fats, including the conjugated forms, differ from industrial ones in their effects. [18]

The look people are after is a leaner trunk and clearer muscle definition at a given body weight, with some also hoping to hold on to lean mass during a cut. Reviews of trial data describe the measured changes in fat mass as small and inconsistent, and the Memorial Sloan Kettering page says CLA does not appear to add to the effects of exercise. [12]

The isomers have distinct effects. Reviews of the biologically active isomers describe c9,t11 as the principal dietary form and attribute lipid and body-composition effects in animals mainly to t10,c12. [2][4][8]

Animal studies have also examined effects on glucose tolerance in diabetic rats and on atherosclerosis in rabbits. [19][20] Wikipedia notes that insulin-related effects in diabetic rats have not been shown in humans. [1]

The t10,c12 isomer has been linked in animals to reduced fat deposition and, in the 1997 mouse study, to higher activity of carnitine palmitoyltransferase, an enzyme involved in moving fatty acids into mitochondria. [3][4] Reviews describe additional proposed actions on lipid metabolism, adipocyte biology and inflammation, and note that effects differ by isomer, species, dose and diet. [8][9] Researchers studying a 12-week human trial used plasma metabolomics to examine which baseline metabolic profiles predicted who responded in body composition and who did not. [21]

Studies of milk-fat synthesis in dairy cows add a related line of work: some diets that alter rumen fermentation raise trans-10,cis-12 CLA and depress milk fat, and this phenomenon has been used as a model for how the isomer influences fat synthesis. [6]

Several small human trials have been registered, including studies of CLA on body fat in overweight children (NCT00575991, 62 participants), body weight and fat oxidation in obese people (NCT00204932, 53 participants), obese women (NCT02529046) and adults with a BMI of 25 or above (NCT04641494, 58 participants). [22][23][24][25] Other registered trials have tested CLA in type 2 diabetes, asthma, breast cancer tissue and advanced solid tumours. [26][27]

Wikipedia summarises the evidence as follows: a 2015 review found no conclusive evidence of benefit for human health, a 2012 meta-analysis found no long-term body-composition effect in overweight or obese people, and a 2018 meta-analysis of randomised trials reported increases in the inflammatory markers CRP and TNF-alpha. [1]

Memorial Sloan Kettering summarises the human evidence on body fat as limited and mixed: some trials report modest fat loss and others none, and CLA does not appear to add to the benefits of exercise. [12] A 2016 double-blind trial in 65 older adults gave a rumenic-acid-rich CLA supplement for eight weeks and examined cognitive function and handgrip performance. [28] A 12-week randomized, placebo-controlled trial of CLA and body composition has been used to study plasma metabolome changes linked to body composition response. [21]

Several human trials have focused on safety markers. Randomized trials reported that CLA raised C-reactive protein, impaired endothelial function and increased markers of lipid peroxidation. [29][30][31] Memorial Sloan Kettering reports that, in obese men with metabolic syndrome, CLA reduced insulin sensitivity, and that it may lower triacylglycerols while raising total cholesterol and lowering HDL. [12]

The US FDA classed CLA as generally recognised as safe for use in foods in 2008. The US and Codex Alimentarius exempt conjugated trans bonds from trans-fat labelling rules. [1] A 2002 study cited by Wikipedia linked isomer-dependent oxidative stress and raised CRP to CLA supplementation. [1]

Reported side effects include fatigue and gastrointestinal symptoms, and case reports describe severe migraine, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome in a woman using a CLA-containing weight-loss product, and acute hepatitis in a 26-year-old woman using CLA for weight loss. [12] The same page advises caution for people with diabetes or cardiovascular risk. [12]

Research continues on individual isomers, their roles in lipid metabolism and the effect of dietary versus supplement sources. Wikipedia notes that research on its biological activity began after a 1979 finding that CLA inhibited chemically induced cancer in mice. [1]

Active questions include whether individual isomers behave differently from mixtures in humans, how supplement doses compare with dietary intake, and whether baseline metabolic profile predicts response. [21][9] Studies of CLA-enriched meat, dairy and eggs continue to examine cancer-related endpoints in cells and animals. [7]

lore.intro: On strength and physique forums CLA is discussed both as a capsule for dropping body fat and as a nutrient in butter and grass-fed beef; posters regularly cite the review literature when arguing either way. [11][15][13]

Ha, Grimm and Pariza report that CLA inhibits chemically induced tumours in mice, opening research on its biological activity (the date as cited on Wikipedia). [1]
A mouse study reports markedly lower body fat and higher lean mass with dietary CLA. [3]
The trans-10,cis-12 isomer is identified as responsible for body-composition changes in mice. [4]
A Journal of Lipid Research review of CLA for obesity notes the supplements are widely promoted as weight-loss agents; it circulates on strength forums. [11]
US FDA categorises CLA as generally recognised as safe for foods. [1]
